Unequal slits give unequal amplitudes, so the two waves can no longer **cancel
completely** - the dark fringes are no longer perfectly dark.
**Step 1 — see what equal slits give.** Equal widths mean equal amplitudes a:
bright: (a + a)² = **4a²** ✓
dark: (a − a)² = **0** ✓ perfect darkness.
**Step 2 — see what unequal slits give.** Amplitudes a₁ ≠ a₂:
bright: **(a₁ + a₂)²** ✓
dark: **(a₁ − a₂)² ≠ 0** ✓ some light remains.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The **dark fringes are not perfectly dark** ✓
**Why the fringes still appear.** The path difference, and hence the **positions** of
maxima and minima, depend only on **d**, **D** and **λ** ✓ Nothing about the slit widths
enters β = λD/d, so the fringes are neither destroyed nor shifted nor unevenly spaced.
Statements (b) and (d) are therefore wrong.
**Why the bright fringes keep equal brightness.** Each maximum has the same amplitude
a₁ + a₂ ✓ (ignoring the slow single-slit envelope). Statement (a) is wrong for the same
reason: it is the **dark** fringes that change, not the bright.
**The quantity that measures this.** The **fringe visibility**,
V = (I_max − I_min)/(I_max + I_min) ✓
With equal slits I_min = 0 and V = **1**, perfect contrast. With unequal slits V < 1,
and the pattern looks washed out.
**A worked instance.** Let a₂ = a₁/2:
I_max ∝ (1·5a₁)² = **2·25a₁²** ✓
I_min ∝ (0·5a₁)² = **0·25a₁²** ✓
V = (2·25 − 0·25)/(2·25 + 0·25) = **0·8** ✓ good contrast still, but the dark fringes
now carry a ninth of the bright intensity.
**In terms of intensities.** With I₁ = 4I₂,
V = 2√(I₁I₂)/(I₁ + I₂) = 2(2I₂)/(5I₂) = **0·8** ✓ the same answer by a second route.
**Why complete cancellation needs equal amplitudes.** Destructive interference removes
only as much as the smaller wave can remove ✓ The excess of the larger wave must go
somewhere, and it appears as residual light at the minima.
**Where this is exploited.** Interferometers are **balanced** - the beam splitter made
exactly 50:50 - precisely to maximise visibility ✓ A poorly balanced Michelson
interferometer gives fringes that are visible but never fully dark.
**The energy bookkeeping.** Average intensity across the screen is I₁ + I₂, whatever the
balance ✓ Interference redistributes the light; it never creates or destroys it.
∴ the dark fringes are not perfectly dark.

Only a **transverse** wave has a plane of vibration to select, so polarisation proves
light transverse.
**Step 1 — define the two kinds of wave.**
**transverse**: the vibration is **perpendicular** to the direction of travel ✓
**longitudinal**: the vibration is **along** the direction of travel ✓
**Step 2 — ask what polarisation means.** Singling out **one** direction of vibration
from the many available ✓
**Step 3 — see why longitudinal waves cannot be polarised.** There is only **one**
possible direction of vibration - along the ray ✓ Nothing to choose between, so no
polarisation is possible.
**Step 4 — conclude.** Light **can** be polarised, so it must be **transverse** ✓
**Why sound cannot be polarised.** Sound in air is a **longitudinal** pressure wave ✓ No
polaroid, no arrangement of slits, can produce a polarised sound beam - and none ever
has.
**The experiment that settles it.** Two polaroids in series. Parallel: light passes.
**Crossed**: extinction ✓ Rotating one of them through 90° blots out the beam entirely -
inexplicable unless the light has a transverse vibration that can be projected onto an
axis.
**Malus's law, which quantifies it.**
I = **I₀cos²θ** ✓ Measuring I against θ and finding a cos² curve confirms the transverse
picture quantitatively.
**Why interference and diffraction are not enough.** Both occur with **longitudinal**
waves too - sound shows interference between two loudspeakers and diffracts round
corners ✓ They prove light is a **wave**, but say nothing about which kind. Polarisation
is the discriminating test.
**What exactly is vibrating.** The **electric** and **magnetic** fields, both
perpendicular to the ray and to each other ✓ Maxwell's equations require it: an
electromagnetic wave is necessarily transverse in free space.
**Which field defines the polarisation.** By convention the **electric** vector ✓ It is
the one that drives charges in a detector and in the eye, so it is the physically
significant direction.
**Where polarised light is met.** Light reflected from water or glass at the **Brewster
angle** is completely polarised; skylight at 90° to the sun is partly polarised; LCD
screens emit it ✓ Bees navigate by the polarisation pattern of the sky.
**The historical note.** Huygens thought light **longitudinal** ✓ Young and Fresnel
showed, from polarisation, that it is transverse - and Fresnel had to rebuild the wave
theory on that basis.
**Reading the distractors.** **Longitudinal** ✗ is excluded by the very phenomenon.
**Dual** ✗ and **particle** ✗ concern wave-particle duality, which polarisation does
not address ✓
∴ transverse.

Because β = λD/d is **linear** in D, the **change** in fringe width gives λ directly.
**Step 1 — write the fringe width.**
β = **λD/d** ✓
**Step 2 — differentiate with respect to D.** Only D changes, so
Δβ = **λΔD/d** ✓
**Step 3 — rearrange for λ.**
λ = **dΔβ/ΔD** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
λ = (1 x 10⁻³)(3 x 10⁻⁵)/(5 x 10⁻²) ✓
**Step 5 — evaluate.**
= 3 x 10⁻⁸/5 x 10⁻²
= **6 x 10⁻⁷ m**
= **600 nm** ✓
**Why the original distance of 1 m is not needed.** The relation is **linear**, so the
change in β depends only on the **change** in D ✓ The 1 m is given to make the situation
concrete, and as a check: β = (6 x 10⁻⁷)(1)/(10⁻³) = **0·6 mm**, a realistic fringe
width.
**The check by direct calculation.**
at D = 1 m: β = **0·600 mm** ✓
at D = 1·05 m: β = (6 x 10⁻⁷)(1·05)/10⁻³ = **0·630 mm** ✓
difference = **0·030 mm = 3 x 10⁻⁵ m** ✓ exactly as stated.
**Why this is a good way to measure λ.** Measuring a **difference** avoids the need to
locate the fringe pattern's absolute scale ✓ and moving the screen a known 5 cm is far
easier to do accurately than measuring D itself from an ill-defined slit plane.
**Why 600 nm is plausible.** It is **orange-yellow** ✓ close to the sodium doublet at
589 nm, the commonest laboratory source for such experiments.
**The sensitivity of the measurement.** A 3 µm change in fringe width must be measured ✓
which is why a travelling microscope is used, and why one counts **ten** fringes and
divides, rather than measuring one.
**What would change if d were halved.** β would **double**, and so would Δβ ✓ Closer
slits give wider fringes - the inverse dependence that makes d the critical dimension in
the apparatus.
**Why the fringes widen as the screen recedes.** The angular separation λ/d is fixed; the
**linear** separation is that angle times D ✓ so the pattern simply scales with distance,
like a shadow.
**Reading the distractors.** **700**, **400** and **500 nm** ✗ would each require a
different Δβ: 3·5, 2·0 and 2·5 x 10⁻⁵ m respectively ✓
∴ 600.

A narrower slit spreads the pattern **wider** and lets through **less** light.
**Step 1 — write the width of the principal maximum.**
linear width = **2λD/a** ✓
**Step 2 — reduce a.** Width ∝ **1/a** ✓ so the central maximum **increases** in width.
**Step 3 — consider the brightness.** Less light enters the slit, and what enters is
spread over a **larger** area ✓ so the maximum becomes **less bright** - on both counts.
**Step 4 — conclude.** **Increases but becomes less bright** ✓
**Why narrowing the slit widens the pattern.** sin θ = λ/a for the first minimum ✓ The
more tightly the wave is confined in space, the more it spreads in **angle**. This is
the optical form of the **uncertainty principle**: Δy Δp_y ≳ ℏ, with the slit fixing Δy
and the diffraction spread fixing Δp_y.
**How the brightness falls.** The **amplitude** at the centre is proportional to a, so
the peak **intensity** goes as **a²** ✓ while the width goes as 1/a. The product - the
total energy - therefore goes as **a**, as it must, since that is how much light the slit
admits.
**A worked instance.** With λ = 600 nm, D = 1 m:
a = 1 mm: width = **1·2 mm** ✓
a = 0·5 mm: width = **2·4 mm** ✓ double, while the peak intensity is **quartered**.
**The limiting case.** As a → λ the pattern spreads over nearly 180° ✓ and the slit
behaves almost like a point source radiating into the whole half-space - very wide and
very faint.
**The opposite limit.** As a becomes large the pattern shrinks towards a sharp bright
image of the slit ✓ which is why **geometrical optics** works for everyday apertures:
diffraction is there, but on a scale too small to notice.
**Why one cannot have both.** Narrow slit and bright sharp image are **incompatible** ✓
This is the fundamental trade-off of every optical instrument: a spectrometer's slit must
be narrow for resolution and wide for light, and the design is always a compromise.
**The connection to telescopes.** The same physics, with a circular aperture: resolution
improves as the aperture **grows** ✓ which is the whole reason for building large
telescopes. θ = 1·22λ/D.
**Reading the distractors.** Anything that says the width **decreases** ✗ reverses the
1/a dependence - the commonest intuition, and wrong. "**Increases but more bright**" ✗
gets the width right but would violate energy conservation ✓
∴ increases but becomes less bright.

**Interference**, **diffraction** and the **slower speed in a denser medium** all support
the wave theory; scattering does not.
**Step 1 — examine (a) scattering.** A beam loses intensity as particles or molecules
deflect it ✓ This is explicable on **either** picture - photons scattering off molecules
works just as well. **Not** decisive ✗
**Step 2 — examine (b) interference.** Two beams combining to give **darkness** ✓ No
particle theory can make light plus light equal no light. **Decisive** ✓
**Step 3 — examine (c) diffraction.** Light bending into the geometrical shadow and
forming fringes there ✓ Particles travel in straight lines. **Decisive** ✓
**Step 4 — examine (d) the speed in a denser medium.** The wave theory predicts
v_denser = **c/µ**, slower ✓ Newton's corpuscular theory predicted the **opposite**.
**Decisive** ✓
**Step 5 — collect.** **b, c and d** ✓
**Why the speed comparison is the historical crux.** The two theories made **opposite**
predictions, so one experiment could settle the matter ✓ **Foucault**, 1850, measured
light in water at about **0·75c** and ended the debate. Until then the corpuscular theory
had Newton's authority behind it.
**Why scattering is not a wave test.** The **Compton effect** - scattering of X-rays off
electrons - is in fact strong evidence for the **particle** nature ✓ Scattering is
therefore worse than neutral; it points the other way.
**Why interference is the strongest single argument.** Young's double slit, 1801 ✓ The
dark fringes exist where light **would** fall if one slit were covered. Opening a second
slit makes a bright place dark - a thing only superposition of amplitudes can do.
**Why diffraction took longer to establish.** Light's wavelength is so short that the
effects are tiny ✓ **Poisson** objected that Fresnel's theory absurdly predicted a bright
spot at the centre of a circular shadow; **Arago** looked, and the spot was there - which
converted the Academy at a stroke.
**The relation between µ and v.**
µ = **c/v** ✓ so µ_water = 1·33 gives v = 2·26 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and Snell's law
µ = sin i/sin r follows directly from the wave construction.
**What the wave theory cannot do.** The **photoelectric** effect, **black-body**
radiation and the **Compton** effect ✓ which is why the modern answer is duality, not a
victory for either side.
**Reading the distractors.** Every alternative includes **scattering** ✓ Spotting that
one item is not a wave test, and that the speed comparison is, settles the question at
once.
∴ b, c, d.

Diffraction becomes observable only when the obstacle is **of the order of the
wavelength**.
**Step 1 — state the condition.** Appreciable bending requires
a ≈ **λ** ✓
**Step 2 — see why.** The angular spread is
θ ≈ **λ/a** ✓
a **large** obstacle gives θ → 0: a sharp shadow, and ray optics ✓
a **comparable** obstacle gives θ ≈ 1 rad: unmistakable spreading ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The size should be **of the order of the wavelength** ✓
**Why everyday objects cast sharp shadows.** Visible light has λ ≈ **5 x 10⁻⁷ m** ✓ For a
1 cm obstacle, θ = 5 x 10⁻⁵ rad - about **0·05 mm** of blurring at a metre, far too little
to notice. Diffraction is always present; it is simply too small to see.
**Why sound bends round corners so readily.** A 340 Hz note has λ = **1 m** ✓ comparable
with a doorway, so it spreads through nearly 180°. One can hear round a corner but not
see round one - the same physics, different wavelengths.
**Why radio waves follow the ground.** Long waves of hundreds of metres diffract round
hills and over the horizon ✓ while microwaves, with λ of centimetres, need line of sight -
which is why mobile masts must be visible to the handset and AM radio need not be.
**A worked instance.** λ = 600 nm, a = 1 µm:
θ = 6 x 10⁻⁷/10⁻⁶ = **0·6 rad ≈ 34°** ✓ a hugely spread pattern.
With a = 1 mm: θ = **0·0006 rad ≈ 0·03°** ✓ barely detectable.
**Why "much larger than the wavelength" is wrong.** That is the condition for
**geometrical** optics, where diffraction is negligible ✓ - the opposite of what is
wanted.
**Why "λ/2" is too prescriptive.** Diffraction is not a threshold phenomenon ✓ It grows
smoothly as a falls through a few wavelengths; no exact size is required, only the right
**order**.
**Why "no relation to wavelength" is wrong.** The ratio λ/a is the **only** thing that
matters ✓ The same obstacle diffracts X-rays imperceptibly and radio waves enormously.
**Where this is turned to use.** **X-ray crystallography**: λ ≈ 1 Å matches atomic
spacings, so crystals diffract X-rays and the pattern reveals the structure ✓ The same
crystal does nothing to visible light.
∴ should be of the order of wavelength.

Fringe width goes as **λ**, and blue light has the **shorter** wavelength.
**Step 1 — write the fringe width.**
β = **λD/d** ✓
**Step 2 — compare the wavelengths.**
yellow ≈ **580 nm** ✓
blue ≈ **450 nm** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** λ falls, so β falls: the fringes become **narrower** ✓
**The ratio.**
β_blue/β_yellow = 450/580 = **0·78** ✓ the pattern shrinks by about a fifth.
**A worked instance.** With D = 1 m and d = 1 mm:
yellow: β = 5·8 x 10⁻⁷/10⁻³ = **0·58 mm** ✓
blue: β = **0·45 mm** ✓
**Why the brightness is not the issue.** The question is about **fringe width**, which
depends on λ, D and d alone ✓ Whether the pattern looks brighter depends on the lamp's
output and the eye's response, neither of which enters the geometry.
**Why the eye finds blue fringes harder to see.** The eye's sensitivity peaks in the
**green-yellow** at 555 nm and falls steeply towards the blue ✓ so blue fringes look
dimmer even at equal power - but that is physiology, not optics.
**What would make the fringes wider.** A **longer** wavelength (red), a **greater** screen
distance, or **closer** slits ✓ Red light at 700 nm would give 0·70 mm, noticeably wider
than yellow.
**Why violet gives the narrowest fringes.** At 400 nm it is the shortest visible
wavelength ✓ which is also why violet is deviated least by a grating and why it sets the
resolution limit of an optical microscope.
**The effect of immersing the apparatus in water.** λ becomes **λ/µ** ✓ so the fringes
narrow by the factor 1/1·33 - the same kind of change as switching from yellow to blue,
and a neat way of measuring µ.
**The white-light pattern.** Each colour gives its own spacing, so beyond the central
white fringe the fringes **spread into spectra** and soon overlap ✓ Only a few coloured
fringes are visible - the blue ones crowded closest to the centre, exactly as this
question implies.
**Why the central fringe is white.** At zero path difference **all** wavelengths are in
phase ✓ independent of λ, so every colour has its maximum there.
**Reading the distractors.** **Wider** ✗ reverses the dependence. **Brighter** ✗ and
**darker** ✗ answer a question about intensity, not width ✓
∴ narrower.
